items.canonical_answer: An organisational structure is the levels of management and divisions of responsibilities within an organisation. It clarifies who performs each role, who may decide and who reports to whom. This can reduce duplicated work and gaps where everyone assumes someone else is responsible. In a centralised structure most decisions are retained at the centre or higher management levels. In a decentralised structure many decisions are delegated to lower levels. The distinction concerns the location of decision-making authority, not the number of buildings or whether the business uses computers. A structure can combine central financial policy with decentralised local service decisions. Clear roles help accountability, but the chart alone cannot ensure cooperation or competent decisions. Structure should fit the scale, activities and skills of the enterprise.
marking_guidance: Meaning: An organisational structure is the levels of management and divisions of responsibilities within an organisation.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.prompt: Explain why saying “three levels of managers” is not a complete definition of organisational structure. Fictional Otavi Makers also needs to know which roles handle production, finance and sales. [6]
items.canonical_answer: Hierarchy describes ranked levels. Organisational structure includes levels and the division of responsibilities, so the three-level statement omits who does what and reports to whom. Allocating production, finance and sales roles supplies part of the missing structure; counting levels alone cannot do that.
marking_guidance: Error: Hierarchy describes ranked levels.

items.canonical_answer: A centralised structure is a management structure in which most decisions are taken at the centre, or at higher levels of management. It can support consistent policy and senior oversight, especially where decisions carry substantial risk. However, referring routine matters upward can delay a response and overload senior managers. The location of offices is not the test; locate the authority.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A centralised structure is a management structure in which most decisions are taken at the centre, or at higher levels of management.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: A decentralised structure is a management structure in which many decisions are not taken at the centre of the business but are delegated to lower levels of management. It can use local knowledge and reduce waiting for head-office approval. Its effectiveness depends on staff competence, clear limits and coordination; different decisions can otherwise become inconsistent. Senior managers retain overall oversight.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A decentralised structure is a management structure in which many decisions are not taken at the centre of the business but are delegated to lower levels of management.

items.prompt: Define authority to make a business decision. [2]

items.prompt: Explain the owner’s span of control. At fictional Lumi Works, two supervisors report directly to the owner and six workers report to each supervisor. A learner says the owner’s span is fourteen. [6]
items.canonical_answer: The owner’s span is two because the supervisors are the direct reports. The twelve workers report directly to those supervisors. Fourteen counts everyone beneath the owner, including indirect reports, which is not span of control.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between these changes: a fictional owner authorises one supervisor to reorder materials within a limit; later the business permits all branch managers to decide routine local service matters. [6]
items.canonical_answer: The first is a particular act of delegation: authority for a task is given to a subordinate while final responsibility remains above. The wider redistribution across branches describes decentralisation. Delegation helps make decentralisation possible, but one delegated task does not establish that most of the organisation’s decisions have moved to lower levels.

items.canonical_answer: A hierarchy is a system in which people or things are arranged according to their importance or authority. In a business it indicates the ranked levels of roles. It is one feature of organisational structure, which also allocates responsibilities. A higher position in a hierarchy can have fewer direct reports than a lower position.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A hierarchy is a system in which people or things are arranged according to their importance or authority.

items.canonical_answer: Responsibility is a duty or obligation to satisfactorily perform or complete a task and which has a consequent penalty for failure. It concerns what a person is answerable for doing. Clear responsibility helps prevent missed tasks, but staff also need the authority, information and resources necessary to carry them out.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Responsibility is a duty or obligation to satisfactorily perform or complete a task and which has a consequent penalty for failure.

items.canonical_answer: Authority is the right to give orders, make decisions, and enforce compliance. It should be adequate for the responsibility assigned and limited to the role’s scope. Having technical expertise does not itself grant authority to direct every other department.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Authority is the right to give orders, make decisions, and enforce compliance.

items.canonical_answer: Span of control is the number of subordinates working directly under a manager. Count direct reporting relationships, not every worker further down the organisation. A wide span may be manageable with experienced staff doing familiar work; complex tasks or inexperienced staff may require more supervision.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Span of control is the number of subordinates working directly under a manager.

items.canonical_answer: Chain of command is a structure within an organisation which allows instructions to be passed down from senior management to lower levels of management. It describes the formal authority route. Information and reports can travel upward along that route. Several stages can support supervision but may increase delay or distortion.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Chain of command is a structure within an organisation which allows instructions to be passed down from senior management to lower levels of management.

items.canonical_answer: Centralisation means retaining most decision-making at the centre or higher levels of management. It can preserve consistency and let senior staff control major risks, but can reduce lower managers’ discretion and slow matters requiring quick local responses. A business can centralise major investments while delegating routine service decisions.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Centralisation means retaining most decision-making at the centre or higher levels of management.

items.canonical_answer: Delegation is giving a subordinate the authority to perform particular tasks (NB it is the authority to perform a task which is being delegated – not the final responsibility). The delegating manager should specify the task, authority, resources and limits, and retain oversight. Delegation is a specific act; decentralisation describes a wider distribution of decisions throughout the organisation.

items.prompt: Explain how appropriate delegation can relieve Ulima’s purchasing bottleneck. Fictional Ulima Furniture requires the owner’s approval for every small replacement part, even though the workshop head knows the repair work. [6]
items.canonical_answer: The features of a structure interact. Adding supervisors can narrow a manager’s direct span and provide closer support, but it can also add a level to the chain of command. Removing levels may speed formal communication while widening the remaining managers’ spans. Delegation can relieve a bottleneck by authorising a subordinate to decide, but responsibility, resources and limits must be clear. A manager cannot meaningfully expect someone to resolve customer complaints while denying authority to offer any remedy. Central control can preserve consistency for high-risk or expensive decisions; local discretion can improve response where staff understand customers and have the necessary competence. Judge these effects in context because neither a tall nor a flat structure has a guaranteed performance advantage. An organisation chart shows the formal structure, not informal friendships or how well people cooperate. The owner becomes a decision bottleneck. Delegating purchases up to an agreed limit can let the head obtain parts sooner; the owner should monitor spending and retain oversight. Removing the spending limit entirely would create a different risk from authorising routine repairs.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: The features of a structure interact.

items.prompt: Draw a simple organisation chart showing Omano’s stated reporting relationships. Omano Supplies has an owner-manager. Production, sales and finance heads each report to the owner-manager. Workers A and B report to the production head; a sales assistant reports to the sales head; an accounts clerk reports to the finance head. [8]
items.canonical_answer:
To draw a simple organisation chart, identify the most senior position, group positions at the correct levels and join each subordinate to the position it reports to directly. Use role titles rather than a list of names without jobs. Do not connect neighbouring roles merely because they are at the same level: a connecting line would imply a reporting relationship not stated. Keep direct spans distinguishable from all lower-level staff. The chart makes formal authority visible and helps a new worker identify a supervisor, but it does not show the quality of management or the informal communication network. Check the finished chart against each reporting fact. A line accidentally bypassing a supervisor changes the structure even if all job titles are present. ![Omano Supplies reporting structure](diagrams/omano-reporting.png)

Place the owner-manager at the top, the three heads at the second level and their direct staff at the third. The owner-manager’s span is three; the production head’s span is two. There are three levels. The chain from Worker A to the owner-manager goes through the production head, not the sales head.
marking_guidance: Knowledge: To draw a simple organisation chart, identify the most senior position, group positions at the correct levels and join each subordinate to the position it reports to directly.

items.prompt: Explain why expansion may require Kawa to change its structure and what effects could follow. Fictional Kawa Packaging grows from five to twenty staff, but its owner still approves every order and work allocation. Customers are waiting for decisions. [6]
items.canonical_answer: A small owner can coordinate a few staff directly, but growth may increase the number, variety and location of decisions beyond that person’s capacity. Appointing functional managers can introduce specialist skills and clarify responsibility. Delegating routine decisions can let local staff respond sooner and free senior management for wider planning. These changes require competent staff, clear authority and communication. More levels may lengthen the formal chain, increasing delay or distortion; extra managers also cost money. Alternatively, flattening the structure may shorten communication while giving remaining managers wider spans. Expansion does not dictate one correct shape. A business with risky technical work may need closer supervision than one with experienced staff carrying out familiar tasks. Review whether the proposed changes solve the actual overload and whether control remains adequate. Appointing an operations head with authority over routine allocations can reduce delay and provide supervision. The owner should specify decision limits and reporting. Adding a manager without passing any authority would add cost while leaving the original bottleneck in place.
marking_guidance: Starting point: A small owner can coordinate a few staff directly, but growth may increase the number, variety and location of decisions beyond that person’s capacity.

items.prompt: State two bases on which an organisation can group its activities. [2]
items.canonical_answer: Businesses can group work by function, product, market or systems. Functional organisation groups similar activities, such as finance and marketing. Product organisation groups responsibility around different products or product ranges. Market organisation groups work around customer markets, which may be geographical areas or customer types. Systems organisation can use project-based teams bringing different skills together to complete a defined piece of work. These approaches answer different coordination needs and can be combined. A product division may still contain functional specialists. Grouping by function does not, by itself, establish whether decisions are centralised: finance staff can be grouped together while some spending authority is delegated elsewhere. The organisation should make reporting and responsibility clear so that coordination across groups does not become a dispute about who decides.
marking_guidance: Point: Businesses can group work by function, product, market or systems.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: Organisation by function groups jobs and activities according to their role, such as production, finance, marketing or human resources. It pools specialist expertise and can clarify functional responsibility. However, departments may focus on their own targets and coordination between them can be difficult. Functional grouping is not a synonym for decentralisation; decision authority can be retained centrally or delegated.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Organisation by function groups jobs and activities according to their role, such as production, finance, marketing or human resources.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: Organisation by product groups activities around a product or product range. A product head can coordinate the production and sales needs of that range, making responsibility for its performance clearer. Different divisions may duplicate support services, and resources can be contested between products. Use product grouping where distinct ranges need concentrated attention rather than assuming every product needs a separate division.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Organisation by product groups activities around a product or product range.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: Organisation by market groups activity according to the market served, such as geographical areas or customer types. It can focus attention on different local or customer needs. Separate market units may duplicate activities and need common policy to protect consistency. A market-based structure does not prove that local heads have unlimited decision authority.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Organisation by market groups activity according to the market served, such as geographical areas or customer types.
items.provenance: Original author prose derived from the named syllabus objectives; no official question text.

items.canonical_answer: Organisation by systems uses a project-based arrangement in which people with relevant skills work together on a defined project. A project team can coordinate contributions from different functions and focus on a shared result. Clear responsibility is needed where specialists also retain links to their functional departments. When the project ends, people may move to other work. This is an organisational arrangement, not simply installing computer software.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Organisation by systems uses a project-based arrangement in which people with relevant skills work together on a defined project.

items.prompt:
Fictional Tuli Foods has expanded. The general manager currently approves routine work allocations and delays occur. The proposed chart puts the general manager above production, sales and finance heads. A production team reports to the production head, a sales assistant to the sales head and an accounts clerk to the finance head. The heads know their functional work well, but spending limits have not yet been agreed.

a(i) Define delegation. [2]
a(ii) State two structural changes that business expansion may require. [2]
b State the meaning of responsibility and the meaning of span of control. [2]
c Explain how Tuli’s proposed reporting structure could help it manage expansion. Include the proposed chart relationships in your explanation. [6]
d Evaluate delegating routine work-allocation decisions to the three heads. [8]
items.canonical_answer: a(i) Giving a subordinate authority for particular tasks while the delegating manager retains final responsibility. a(ii) Appointing specialist managers and passing appropriate decision authority to lower levels. b Responsibility is the duty to complete a task satisfactorily; span is the number of direct subordinates. c Put the general manager at the top and the three heads beneath, then each specified team or assistant directly below the appropriate head. This gives the general manager a direct span of three and clarifies functional supervision. Heads can coordinate their areas, reducing the general manager’s direct workload and giving staff a clear reporting route. An extra level can delay communication, so authority must be real rather than sending all routine decisions upward. d The heads’ functional knowledge supports delegation and their faster work allocations could reduce the stated delays. Against this, undefined spending limits could cause inconsistent or excessive commitments and the general manager remains accountable. Delegate routine allocations with clear boundaries and review arrangements; keep major commitments centrally approved. Adding titles without authority would leave the bottleneck, while unrestricted authority is not needed to solve it.

items.prompt:
Fictional Tuli Foods has expanded. The general manager currently approves routine work allocations and delays occur. The proposed chart puts the general manager above production, sales and finance heads. A production team reports to the production head, a sales assistant to the sales head and an accounts clerk to the finance head. The heads know their functional work well, but spending limits have not yet been agreed.

a Explain what Tuli’s proposed organisation chart would show and how it could improve accountability as the business expands. [8]
b Evaluate retaining central approval of all routine decisions compared with delegating within limits. [12]
items.canonical_answer:
a The chart puts the general manager above the three heads, with each team or assistant under its specified functional head. It has three levels and a direct general-manager span of three. Staff can identify the supervisor responsible for work and where to report problems; heads can be held answerable for their functional activities. The chart clarifies the formal chain and reduces uncertainty about who allocates work, but does not by itself grant discretion or prove effective cooperation. Actual authority and communication must match the boxes and lines.

b Central approval can preserve consistency and allow senior oversight of substantial risk, but approving every routine allocation is already causing delays and leaves knowledgeable heads underused. Delegation can improve response and free the general manager for expansion planning. It also creates a need to specify limits, report performance and coordinate between functions. Delegate routine decisions to the experienced heads within agreed limits because that directly addresses the current bottleneck. Retain central decisions for major commitments and review outcomes. This is preferable to either unrestricted discretion or unchanged approval of every small matter; if competence or control proved inadequate, the delegated limits should be tightened.

items.prompt:
Fictional Nari Repairs has grown to twelve operational staff plus two supervisors. Two experienced supervisors report to the owner and six staff report to each supervisor. Routine work decisions still await the owner, causing delays. The supervisors can make competent routine decisions if authorised within clear limits. The owner is deciding whether to delegate these decisions.

Evaluate delegating routine decisions to Nari’s supervisors under the original facts. Give an answer plan that explains the formal reporting structure. [12]
items.canonical_answer: Structure: owner above two supervisors, each above six staff; owner span two, supervisor span six. Delegation transfers task authority but not the owner’s final responsibility. Benefit: competent supervisors can decide routine matters sooner, relieving the stated delay and allowing the owner to focus on wider needs. Risk: inconsistent choices or poor coordination if boundaries and reporting are unclear. Judgement: delegate within agreed limits and monitor outcomes, because experienced supervisors are available and central approval is the bottleneck. Do not change the owner’s span by counting the twelve indirect reports. The choice depends on competence and control, not on decentralisation being universally superior.

items.prompt:
Fictional Nari Repairs has grown to twelve operational staff plus two supervisors. Two experienced supervisors report to the owner and six staff report to each supervisor. Routine work decisions still await the owner, causing delays. The supervisors can make competent routine decisions if authorised within clear limits. The owner is deciding whether to delegate these decisions. For part (b) only, both experienced supervisors leave and are replaced by newcomers with no supervisory experience. Other facts remain unchanged.

a Evaluate delegated routine decision authority in Nari’s original structure. Describe the chart’s reporting relationships as part of your answer. [12]
b Evaluate the same proposal after the supervisors are replaced by inexperienced newcomers. Explain whether the judgement changes. [12]
items.canonical_answer: a The owner has two direct supervisor reports; each supervisor has six direct staff. The three-level chart defines the chain but current decisions still await the owner. Delegation would let experienced supervisors allocate routine work faster while retaining the owner’s final responsibility. Clear limits and reporting reduce inconsistency, although the owner must still monitor the results. Delegate because the necessary competence is stated and the approval delay is a real constraint. The benefit comes from moving authority, not merely redrawing boxes. b The formal chart and direct spans remain unchanged, but the competence condition has changed. Broad immediate delegation now risks errors and insufficient support for six staff per newcomer. Keeping every decision with the owner would preserve the original delay, so use narrower authority with close checking initially, and develop competence before widening it. On these facts reduce the initial scope of delegation rather than abandoning it permanently. The original wide routine discretion is less justified because experienced judgement is no longer available.
